notes.meaning: The writer urges his own heart to wake up and praise the Lord with deep gratitude. When we look at God's works, we see that He is royal, wrapped in honor and majesty like a great king.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: In Orthodox worship, this psalm opens the evening service of Vespers as man's very first act of worship, meeting God first of all as the Creator of the world.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note striking literary parallels between this psalm and the ancient Egyptian Great Hymn to the Aten, showing how biblical writers engaged and answered surrounding cultures by showing the Lord alone as Creator.

notes.meaning: God covers Himself with bright light as if it were a robe, and unrolls the wide blue sky as easily as someone pitches a tent. Even though our eyes cannot see God directly, the beauty of the visible universe reveals His glorious presence to us.

Here God is pictured as building His upper rooms above the rain clouds and riding through the sky using the storm clouds as His royal chariot. He moves peacefully and swiftly above the world, showing complete mastery over the strongest winds.

God commands the natural forces of wind and lightning as eager servants ready to do His will. The New Testament also applies these words to angels, showing that these mighty spiritual beings are created servants who belong under the authority of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars argue that the original Hebrew poetically describes winds and lightning as God's natural messengers, whereas the ancient Greek translation read them as spiritual angels.

notes.meaning: The Lord placed the earth firmly where He wanted it, keeping it balanced and steady in space by His own power. It will remain completely secure until its earthly purpose is finished and God brings in a new earth.

In the beginning, deep, stormy waters wrapped around the whole earth like a heavy coat, rising higher than the tops of the mountains. The globe was entirely covered with water until God chose to uncover the dry land.

At God's sharp command, the deep waters rushed into their appointed places, leaving mountains to stand tall and valleys to sink down. He set an invisible border at the seashores so that the ocean can never rise again to drown the entire earth.

Instead of letting waters be destructive, God turns them into fresh springs that wind through hills and valleys to refresh living things. Wild donkeys in the lonely desert find drink, and songbirds build nests and sing among the green leafy branches.
High hilltops cannot be reached by flowing rivers, so the Lord waters them straight from the rain clouds above. The whole ground drinks its fill of these showers and blossoms with life.

The Lord makes green pasture for farm animals and gives crops for people to cultivate and harvest for food. He generously provides bread to give real physical strength, olive oil to soothe the skin and brighten the face, and wine to cheer the human heart.

God provides for wild plants and creatures far beyond human gardens, giving deep sap to the giant cedars and homes to nesting storks. Even high, jagged cliffs give a safe refuge to wild goats and small rock badgers.

The moon marks out months and religious feast days, and the sun always sets precisely at its appointed time. Far from being gods to worship, these heavenly lights are simply faithful clocks set in motion by the Creator.

Night is created by God so that the earth can rest and wild animals can safely hunt in the dark. When young lions roar across the wilderness, their natural cries are treated by God as an appeal to Him to provide their daily meat.

When the morning sun appears, the predatory animals slip quietly back to their dens to sleep. With the dangerous beasts tucked away, people can safely step outside to do their honest daily work until evening comes.

Looking across all these wonders, the psalmist is filled with awe at how many different things God has made. Every creature was shaped with perfect divine wisdom, and the whole world is packed full of His riches.

The ocean spreads out vast and wide, teeming with countless swimming creatures both tiny and huge. Human ships sail upon it to connect distant lands, while Leviathan, the great sea monster or whale, splashes and plays safely in the waves.

Every creature on land and sea waits like a hungry child for God to supply its daily meal at the right time. When He scatters His bounty, they gather it up, and when He opens His generous hand, they are completely satisfied.
All living things rely entirely on God's kindness every moment. If He hides His favor, they are thrown into panic, and if He takes away their breath, they die instantly and crumble back to dust.

When God sends out His breath or Spirit, brand-new generations are brought to life, filling the places left by those that died. In this way, His continuing care continually refreshes and renews the face of the earth, just like springtime after a long winter.

differ.view: John Gill taught that this verse points to the work of the Holy Spirit, who not only renews dead souls in conversion but will also bring about a glorious new creation at the end of time.

notes.meaning: The psalmist prays that God's eternal glory may shine forever and never fade away. Just as the Creator rested on the seventh day and was delighted with what He made, He continues to take genuine pleasure in His good creation.

Even though God is deeply loving, He possesses breathtaking power over all the earth. A single glance from Him makes the ground shake like an earthquake, and a mere touch can cause mountains to smoke and burn with volcanic fire.

Because God gives us life and keeps us alive, the writer makes a personal promise to sing praises to the Lord for as long as he lives. Believers look forward to praising their covenant God both throughout this earthly life and on into eternity.

Thinking quietly and deeply about God's goodness brings true sweetness and comfort to the believer's soul. In return, the Lord is delighted when His people fix their thoughts on Him and find their greatest joy in who He is.

Rebellion and sin are the only ugly stains on God's wonderful creation, so the psalmist longs for wickedness to be completely removed from the earth. The psalm ends as it began, calling the soul to bless the Lord, and adding the joyful cry, Hallelujah, which means 'Praise the Lord.'
